title: The pointer
hookLine: the reader follows the words with a silver hand, so the scroll isn't touched

lines: A TOOL SHAPED LIKE A HAND.
cards: Here is the job description. Read aloud, in front of a full room, from a page with no punctuation, no vowels, no verse numbers, and no notes on how to sing it.
Just columns of black Hebrew letters, written by hand on parchment, in a text the room expects to hear without a single word wrong. And no putting a finger on the line to keep your place.
That's the Torah reader's job, week after week. And there's a small tool on the table to help, shaped like a hand.

teach.b: It's called a yad: Hebrew for hand. A slim rod, often silver, sometimes wood, ending in a tiny hand with one finger pointing. The reader holds it just above the parchment and moves it word by word.
Why not just use a finger? Two reasons. First, the scroll itself is fragile, and treated as holy.

teach.h: A SMUDGED LETTER, AN UNFIT SCROLL.
teach.b: Every letter is written by a trained scribe, a sofer, with a quill and special ink, and a smudged or broken letter can make the whole scroll unfit until it's repaired. Hands carry oil and sweat.

Second, there's a teaching in the Talmud, in Megillah 32a, that holding a Torah scroll with bare hands is a kind of disrespect. So people touch it with something else: the fringe of a tallit, the cover, or the yad.
The yad itself is a custom, not a law spelled out in the Talmud, but today it's a familiar sight at the reading table.

teach.h: NO VOWELS, NO NOTES: PREPARED BY HEART.
teach.b: Because the scroll has no vowels or musical notes, the reader prepares well ahead.
In many synagogues, two people stand on either side, following in a printed book with all the vowels and notes, ready to quietly correct a mistake.
And the person called up to bless the reading touches the place with their tallit fringe and kisses it. The yad teaches something without a word.

teach.h: THE POINT IS WHAT IT POINTS TO.

teach.b: It's what the hand points to.

how: During the Torah reading, the reader follows the text with a yad, a pointer ending in a small hand, while gabbaim follow in a printed chumash and correct errors; those called up touch the scroll with a tallit fringe or its cover and kiss it.

games.q: you're reading Torah in front of the congregation and need to keep your place on the parchment. what do you do?
o: run your finger along the line.
follow the words with a yad, just above the parchment.
games.why: the yad keeps your place without touching the parchment, protecting the letters and honoring the scroll.

practice: Pick up something written, a book, a letter, a page of scripture, even a recipe, and read a few lines slowly, moving your finger or a pen just under each word.
Don't let your eyes run ahead of your hand; notice the small words and odd spellings you'd usually skim. If it's a sacred text for you, let the pointing be a kind of respect.

wordCard.voice: Yad. Hand. The pointer the Torah reader uses to follow the words without touching the parchment.

carryVoice: Your line: a hand that points. A good teacher, parent or friend works the same way. That's day five hundred ninety-eight.
